newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: FORECAST-Irish mid-November CPI to remain subdued.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Irish mid-November CPI to remain subdued.

text.p: Ireland's consumer price index for the quarter to mid-November, due for release at 1200 GMT on Thursday, should show price pressures in the Irish economy remain subdued, analysts said.
But the data will be closely scrutinised for any sign that the impact of the punt's drop against sterling in recent weeks is feeding through to Irish inflation, they said.

A survey of eight Irish analysts showed they expected a rise of between 0.3 percent and 0.5 percent in consumer prices on the quarter while year-on-year forecasts ranged from 1.7 percent to 1.9 percent. "Some of the impact of the decline of the punt against sterling could yet be felt," said Ulster Bank economist Eoin Fahy, who is forecasting a 0.5 percent increase in prices on the quarter for a year-on-year rise of 1.9 percent.
But others say it may be too early to see any currency effect on the figures and the market may have to wait until January to see the impact of punt/sterling weakness.
"The data will probably be inconclusive and the market may have to wait for figures early next year when CPI data will be published on a monthly basis," Davy Stockbrokers said.
Davy is forecasting a quarterly rise of 0.4 percent for a 1.8 percent increase year-on-year.
The punt fell by nearly 3.5 percent against sterling, a key currency in determining Irish import prices, in the period between mid-August and mid-November.
Analysts said although food price inflation was subdued the punt's drop against sterling may have impacted on prices of imports from Britain such as clothing and footware.

"The outcome is a trade-off between these two factors. But we are not too far from German inflation and this is acceptable," said Padhraic Garvey of Riada Stockbrokers, who is looking for a 0.4 percent rise in prices on the quarter for a 1.8 percent increase year-on-year.
"This should go down well in the market because this will confirm that Irish inflation is below two percent and this is a key level," Garvey told Reuters.
Marginal increases are expected in things such as television licences and electronics.
Analysts said the strong growth rate of the Irish economy had pushed its inflation rate in Europe higher than most countries and means the figures will be closely watched by the market.

"The increase in economic growth has meant Irish inflation is near the top of the range of price increases in Europe. The market is watching the year-on-year figure very carefully and it will be very important to us," said John Beggs, economist at AIB Group Treasury. He is forecasting a mid-November increase of 0.4 percent for 1.8 percent year-on-year.
Analysts say a figure under two percent should be well received by the market but anything above that could cause concern.

"The market's reaction should be fairly muted. The quarterly figures should not be too bad and nothing too dramatic will happen unless the year-on-year figure goes to two percent," said Alan McQuaid of Bloxham brokers who sees the CPI rising 1.8 percent year-on-year.
